stem: A used-car market has 600 buyers, each willing to buy at most one car, and 500 sellers, each owning one car. There are 400 good cars (peaches) and 100 bad cars (lemons). Buyers value a peach at Rs.100 and a lemon at Rs.10. Sellers value their own peach at Rs.50 or their own lemon at Rs.10. Sellers know their car's quality; buyers know only the aggregate numbers and all valuations. What outcome maximizes aggregate surplus? Explain. [4 marks]
answer: Trade all 400 peaches; lemon trade is optional. Maximum gains from trade are Rs.20,000.
solution: Trading a peach generates a gain of $100-50=50$, while trading a lemon generates $10-10=0$. There are enough buyers to buy all 500 cars, so no beneficial peach transaction needs to be crowded out by another trade. Thus every peach should move from its seller to a buyer, generating $400\cdot50=20{,}000$. Any number of lemons may also trade without changing aggregate gains from trade. This is the gains-from-trade surplus, relative to sellers retaining their cars.
hint: Compare buyer value with seller opportunity cost for each quality.

stem: A used-car market has 600 buyers, each willing to buy at most one car, and 500 sellers, each owning one car. There are 400 good cars (peaches) and 100 bad cars (lemons). Buyers value a peach at Rs.100 and a lemon at Rs.10. Sellers value their own peach at Rs.50 or their own lemon at Rs.10. Sellers know their car's quality; buyers know only the aggregate numbers and all valuations. (i) Derive the supply of used cars as a function of price, and draw it with quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis. (ii) Derive and draw demand in the same figure. Label all important points. (iii) Find all competitive equilibria and identify the qualities traded. [20 marks]
answer: With weak participation at reservation prices: price 10 with any quantity from 0 to 100 lemons; price 50 with 100 lemons and 80 peaches; or price 82 with all 500 cars.
solution:
Supply is a correspondence: $S(p)=0$ for $p<10$; $S(10)=[0,100]$; $S(p)=100$ for $10<p<50$; $S(50)=[100,500]$; and $S(p)=500$ for $p>50$. Plot horizontal supply segments at prices 10 and 50, with vertical segments at quantities 0, 100 and 500 as appropriate.

Demand must use the quality mix of cars actually offered. A lemon-only pool is worth 10 per car. If all 100 lemons and $k$ peaches are offered, the expected buyer value is $v(k)=(1000+100k)/(100+k)$. For a given pool, demand is 600 below its expected value, zero above it, and any amount in $[0,600]$ at equality. Equivalently, for offered quantity $q>100$, the zero-surplus buyer valuation curve is $p=100-9000/q$, rising from $(q,p)=(100,10)$ to $(500,82)$; for a lemon-only pool it is $p=10$.

At $p=10$, sellers and buyers of lemons are indifferent, so any quantity $q\in[0,100]$ of lemons can clear; if indifference is resolved in favour of full participation, $q=100$. At $p=50$, all lemons are supplied and peach sellers are indifferent. Setting $v(k)=50$ gives $k=80$, so $q=180$ clears. At $p>50$, every car is supplied and expected quality value is $(400\cdot100+100\cdot10)/500=82$. Thus $p=82$, with 500 buyers trading and 100 abstaining, is the full-pooling equilibrium. No other prices clear: on $(10,50)$ only overpriced lemons are offered, and outside these boundary cases demand and supply disagree.
hint: At price 50, peach sellers are indifferent; do not automatically assume all 400 peaches must be offered. Match buyers' expected value to the actual offered pool.
notes: Reservation-price indifference is handled as a correspondence. A convention forcing all indifferent sellers to trade removes the partial-peach equilibrium at p=50 and fixes lemon-only trade at 100. The source does not specify such a tie-breaking convention. Demand is conditional on offered quality, so an unconditional single-valued demand curve is not well-defined without a selection convention.

stem: A used-car market has 600 buyers, each willing to buy at most one car, and 500 sellers, each owning one car. There are 400 good cars (peaches) and 100 bad cars (lemons). Buyers value a peach at Rs.100 and a lemon at Rs.10. Sellers value their own peach at Rs.50 or their own lemon at Rs.10. Sellers know their car's quality; buyers know only the aggregate numbers and all valuations. Now buyers also know each individual car's quality. Use demand and supply analysis to find all competitive equilibria. [6 marks]
answer: All 400 peaches trade at price 100. Lemons have price 10 and any traded quantity in $[0,100]$, under weak participation.
solution: With quality observable, buyers can choose peach and lemon markets separately. At a peach price below 100, each of the 600 buyers strictly prefers a peach to abstaining or a fairly priced lemon. Since there are only 400 peaches, a lower price cannot clear. At price 100 buyers are indifferent and 400 of them can be assigned peaches; all peach sellers strictly prefer selling because 100 exceeds 50. Thus $p_P=100$, $q_P=400$. In the lemon market both buyer value and seller opportunity cost are 10, so $p_L=10$, with any quantity $q_L\in[0,100]$ under indifference; at most 100 of the remaining 200 buyers are needed. Full participation gives $q_L=100$. These allocations achieve the efficient Rs.20,000 gains from peach trade.
hint: Observable quality creates separate peach and lemon markets. There are more peach buyers than peach sellers.

stem: A private firm $r$ and a public firm $u$ choose nonnegative quantities $q_r,q_u$ of a homogeneous good. Inverse demand is $p=a-bQ$, where $Q=q_r+q_u$, $a,b>0$. Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. Derive (i) each firm's profit, (ii) consumer surplus, and (iii) welfare, defined as consumer plus producer surplus. [5 marks]
solution: Revenue minus cost gives $\pi_r=(a-b(q_r+q_u)-c)q_r$ and $\pi_u=(a-b(q_r+q_u)-c)q_u$. The area below inverse demand and above market price is $CS=\int_0^Q(a-bz)\,dz-pQ=bQ^2/2$. Adding profits cancels transfers through the price and gives $W=\int_0^Q(a-bz)\,dz-cQ=(a-c)Q-bQ^2/2$.
hint: Consumer surplus is a triangle; total welfare equals gross willingness to pay minus production cost.

stem: A private firm $r$ and a public firm $u$ choose nonnegative quantities $q_r,q_u$ of a homogeneous good. Inverse demand is $p=a-bQ$, where $Q=q_r+q_u$, $a,b>0$. Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. For given $q_u$, set up the private firm's profit maximization problem and derive its reaction function. [3 marks]
solution: The private firm solves $\max_{q_r\geq0}(a-c-bq_u-bq_r)q_r$. The interior first-order condition is $a-c-bq_u-2bq_r=0$, and the second derivative is $-2b<0$. Enforcing nonnegativity yields $BR_r(q_u)=\max\{(a-c-bq_u)/(2b),0\}$.
hint: Differentiate private profit with respect to $q_r$, holding $q_u$ fixed.

stem: A private firm $r$ and a public firm $u$ choose nonnegative quantities $q_r,q_u$ of a homogeneous good. Inverse demand is $p=a-bQ$, where $Q=q_r+q_u$, $a,b>0$. Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. For given $q_r$, set up the public firm's welfare maximization problem and derive its reaction function. [3 marks]
solution: The public firm solves $\max_{q_u\geq0}(a-c)(q_r+q_u)-\frac b2(q_r+q_u)^2$. Its interior first-order condition is $a-c-b(q_r+q_u)=0$; the second derivative is $-b<0$. Therefore $BR_u(q_r)=\max\{(a-c)/b-q_r,0\}$.
hint: The public firm chooses total output to equate inverse demand with marginal production cost.

stem: A private firm $r$ and a public firm $u$ choose nonnegative quantities $q_r,q_u$ of a homogeneous good. Inverse demand is $p=a-bQ$, where $Q=q_r+q_u$, $a,b>0$. Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. Define equilibrium under quantity competition, find equilibrium outputs, price, profits, consumer surplus and welfare, and illustrate it using reaction functions with $q_u$ on the horizontal axis and $q_r$ on the vertical axis. [11 marks]
answer: $q_r^*=0$, $q_u^*=(a-c)/b$, $p^*=c$, both profits zero, and $CS^*=W^*=(a-c)^2/(2b)$.
solution: A Nash equilibrium is a pair of quantities at which neither firm can improve its objective by changing its own quantity while holding the other's fixed. Put $A=(a-c)/b>0$. The reactions are $q_r=\max\{(A-q_u)/2,0\}$ and $q_u=\max\{A-q_r,0\}$. If the public output is positive, substituting $q_u=A-q_r$ into the private reaction gives $q_r=q_r/2$, hence $q_r=0$ and $q_u=A$. A corner with $q_u=0$ cannot be an equilibrium because the private best response is $A/2$, at which the public firm wants $A/2>0$. Thus the stated equilibrium is unique. Total output is $A$, price is $a-bA=c$, and each firm's margin and profit are zero. Consumer surplus and welfare are $bA^2/2=(a-c)^2/(2b)$. In the requested graph the private reaction joins $(0,A/2)$ to $(A,0)$ before lying along the horizontal axis; the positive public reaction is the line from $(0,A)$ to $(A,0)$. Their equilibrium intersection is $(q_u,q_r)=(A,0)$.
hint: Intersect the two reaction functions, including nonnegative-output corners.
notes: Question 2(d) starts on PDF page11 and continues on page12.

stem: A private firm $r$ and a public firm $u$ choose nonnegative quantities $q_r,q_u$ of a homogeneous good. Inverse demand is $p=a-bQ$, where $Q=q_r+q_u$, $a,b>0$. Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. The private firm's marginal cost falls to $c_r<c$, while public marginal cost remains $c$. Draw the new reaction functions and explain how $q_r,q_u,Q$, price, both profits, consumer surplus and welfare change. Exact expressions are not required. [8 marks]
answer: Private output and profit rise; public output falls (possibly to zero). Total output and consumer surplus weakly rise, price weakly falls, public profit remains zero, and welfare rises.
solution: The public reaction remains $q_u=\max\{(a-c)/b-q_r,0\}$, because the effect of its own output on welfare is still $p-c$. The private reaction shifts upward to $q_r=\max\{(a-c_r-bq_u)/(2b),0\}$. Let $\delta=c-c_r>0$ and $A=(a-c)/b$. If $\delta\leq a-c$, the intersection is $q_r=\delta/b$ and $q_u=A-\delta/b$. Thus output shifts from the public firm to the cheaper private firm while $Q=A$, $p=c$ and consumer surplus remain unchanged. Private profit becomes $\delta^2/b>0$, public profit remains zero, and welfare rises by the production-cost saving $\delta^2/b$.\n\nIf the cost fall is so large that $\delta>a-c$, the public firm reaches its zero-output corner. The private firm then produces $(a-c_r)/(2b)>A$ and charges $(a+c_r)/2<c$. Total output and consumer surplus rise strictly; private profit and welfare rise, while public profit remains zero because its output is zero. The second regime matters because the question does not restrict the size of the cost reduction.
hint: The public reaction is unchanged. Check whether its new intersection with the shifted private reaction still has nonnegative public output.

stem: A unit mass of consumers each buys at most one unit. Consumer valuation $v$ is uniform on $[0,1]$. A monopoly has total cost $q^3$ and initially cannot identify consumers, so must set one uniform price. Derive demand as a function of price. [6 marks]
answer: $q(p)=1$ for $p\leq0$, $q(p)=1-p$ for $0<p<1$, and $q(p)=0$ for $p\geq1$.
solution: A consumer buys when $v\geq p$. For $0<p<1$, the uniform distribution puts mass $1-p$ above $p$, so demand is $1-p$. At a nonpositive price all consumers buy, while a price at least 1 generates zero demand except for a measure-zero indifferent endpoint. Economically relevant nonnegative prices therefore give inverse demand $p=1-q$ for $0\leq q\leq1$.
hint: Count the consumers whose valuation exceeds the price.

stem: A unit mass of consumers each buys at most one unit. Consumer valuation $v$ is uniform on $[0,1]$. A monopoly has total cost $q^3$ and initially cannot identify consumers, so must set one uniform price. Derive the monopoly price and profit. [4 marks]
solution: Using inverse demand, profit is $\pi(q)=(1-q)q-q^3$. The first derivative is $1-2q-3q^2$, which vanishes at $q=1/3$ (the other root is -1). The second derivative $-2-6q$ is strictly negative on $[0,1]$, so this is the unique maximum. Consequently $p=1-q=2/3$ and $\pi=2/9-1/27=5/27$.
hint: Maximize revenue minus cost using $p=1-q$.

stem: A unit mass of consumers each buys at most one unit. Consumer valuation $v$ is uniform on $[0,1]$. A monopoly has total cost $q^3$ and initially cannot identify consumers, so must set one uniform price. For a cost the firm can learn whether a consumer's valuation is in $[0,4/5]$ or in $(4/5,1]$. What is the maximum amount it is willing to pay for this information? Explain. [20 marks]
answer: The maximum payment is $(46\sqrt{115}-472)/675\approx0.0315482$.
solution: With information the firm can price separately to the two groups. Let $l\in[0,4/5]$ and $h\in[0,1/5]$ be quantities sold to the low- and high-valuation groups. Inverse group demands are $p_L=4/5-l$ and $p_H=1-h$. The profit objective is $(4/5-l)l+(1-h)h-(l+h)^3$, a strictly concave function over the rectangle of feasible quantities.\n\nAn unrestricted interior solution would require $4/5-2l=1-2h=3(l+h)^2$. It gives $h>1/5$, which is infeasible. The optimum therefore serves the entire high group: $h=1/5$, at $p_H=4/5$. If $Q=l+1/5$, the remaining first-order condition is $4/5-2l=3Q^2$, or $3Q^2+2Q-6/5=0$. Thus $Q=(\sqrt{115}-5)/15$ and $l=(\sqrt{115}-8)/15$. Low-group price is $p_L=1-Q=(20-\sqrt{115})/15$. The high-group marginal revenue at its upper quantity is $3/5$, exceeding marginal cost $3Q^2$, as required for this boundary optimum. Substitution yields informed profit $(46\sqrt{115}-347)/675\approx0.2167334$. Subtracting the uninformed profit $5/27$ gives the willingness to pay $(46\sqrt{115}-472)/675\approx0.0315482$.
hint: Use separate inverse demands for the two groups, but a cost depending on total output. Check the high group's quantity cap of $1/5$.

stem: In a short-run AD-AS model capital is fixed at $\bar K$. Production is $Y=AL+\bar K$, $A>0$. The union fixes a minimum nominal wage $\bar W$. Each of the $\bar L$ workers supplies one unit if $W>\bar W$, supplies none if $W<\bar W$, and is indifferent at equality. Aggregate demand is a standard downward-sloping curve. Derive aggregate labour supply as a function of nominal wage $W$. [4 marks]
answer: $L^S(W)=0$ below $\bar W$, $[0,\bar L]$ at $\bar W$, and $\bar L$ above $\bar W$.
solution: All workers have the same reservation nominal wage. Below it none supplies labour. Above it every worker supplies the endowed unit. At exactly $\bar W$, any number from zero to the available workforce may supply because workers are indifferent. With employment on the horizontal axis and nominal wage on the vertical axis, supply has a horizontal segment at $\bar W$ between 0 and $\bar L$, and a vertical segment at $L=\bar L$ above it.
hint: Distinguish strict inequality from the indifference case at the reservation wage.

stem: In a short-run AD-AS model capital is fixed at $\bar K$. Production is $Y=AL+\bar K$, $A>0$. The union fixes a minimum nominal wage $\bar W$. Each of the $\bar L$ workers supplies one unit if $W>\bar W$, supplies none if $W<\bar W$, and is indifferent at equality. Aggregate demand is a standard downward-sloping curve. (i) Derive aggregate labour demand as a function of the real wage $W/P$. (ii) Derive it as a function of nominal wage $W$ for given $P$. [6 marks]
answer: Desired labour is zero if $W/P>A$, arbitrary nonnegative if $W/P=A$, and unbounded if $W/P<A$; in nominal terms compare $W$ with $PA$.
solution: The labour-dependent part of competitive profit is $(PA-W)L$. If $W/P>A$, every extra worker loses money, so desired employment is zero. If $W/P=A$, every nonnegative employment level yields the same labour profit. If $W/P<A$, the linear technology gives a positive constant profit per extra worker and hence no finite unconstrained maximizer: desired labour is unbounded. The finite workforce constrains realized equilibrium employment, not unconstrained desired labour. For a fixed price level, replace the comparison $W/P$ versus $A$ with $W$ versus $PA$. The inverse labour-demand curve is horizontal at $W=PA$.
hint: The marginal product is constant. Examine the sign of the marginal profit from another worker.
notes: Part4(b)(ii) continues on PDF page13. Unbounded desired demand below the marginal-product wage should not be confused with the finite available workforce.

stem: In a short-run AD-AS model capital is fixed at $\bar K$. Production is $Y=AL+\bar K$, $A>0$. The union fixes a minimum nominal wage $\bar W$. Each of the $\bar L$ workers supplies one unit if $W>\bar W$, supplies none if $W<\bar W$, and is indifferent at equality. Aggregate demand is a standard downward-sloping curve. Draw labour supply and demand for an arbitrary $P$, using $L$ on the horizontal axis and $W$ on the vertical axis. Derive equilibrium employment as a function of $P$. [10 marks]
answer: $L^*=0$ if $P<\bar W/A$, $L^*\in[0,\bar L]$ at equality, and $L^*=\bar L$ if $P>\bar W/A$.
solution: For fixed $P$, inverse demand is the horizontal line $W=PA$. Supply is horizontal at $\bar W$ over $0\leq L\leq\bar L$ and vertical at the full workforce above that wage. If $PA<\bar W$, no mutually acceptable wage supports positive labour: firms will not pay the reservation wage, and workers will not accept their marginal revenue product. Equilibrium employment is zero. If $PA>\bar W$, labour-market clearing requires $W=PA$ and all $\bar L$ workers are employed. If $PA=\bar W$, both sides are indifferent, so any employment between 0 and $\bar L$ clears at that wage. These are the stated cases after dividing by $A>0$.
hint: Compare the horizontal demand line at $PA$ with the reservation-wage line at $\bar W$.

stem: In a short-run AD-AS model capital is fixed at $\bar K$. Production is $Y=AL+\bar K$, $A>0$. The union fixes a minimum nominal wage $\bar W$. Each of the $\bar L$ workers supplies one unit if $W>\bar W$, supplies none if $W<\bar W$, and is indifferent at equality. Aggregate demand is a standard downward-sloping curve. Derive aggregate supply $Y$ as a function of $P$, and draw it with $Y$ on the horizontal axis and $P$ on the vertical axis. [5 marks]
answer: Supply is $\bar K$ below $P_0=\bar W/A$, any $Y\in[\bar K,\bar K+A\bar L]$ at $P_0$, and $\bar K+A\bar L$ above $P_0$.
solution: Substitute equilibrium employment into $Y=AL+\bar K$. Below $P_0=\bar W/A$ employment is zero and output is $\bar K$. At $P_0$, any employment from zero to full employment is possible, so output lies in $[\bar K,\bar K+A\bar L]$. Above $P_0$, full-employment output is $\bar K+A\bar L$. The requested graph has a lower-price vertical segment at $Y=\bar K$, a horizontal segment at $P=P_0$ joining $\bar K$ to $\bar K+A\bar L$, and an upper-price vertical segment at $Y=\bar K+A\bar L$.
hint: Translate each employment regime into output through the production function.

stem: In a short-run AD-AS model capital is fixed at $\bar K$. Production is $Y=AL+\bar K$, $A>0$. The union fixes a minimum nominal wage $\bar W$. Each of the $\bar L$ workers supplies one unit if $W>\bar W$, supplies none if $W<\bar W$, and is indifferent at equality. Aggregate demand is a standard downward-sloping curve. Explain the effectiveness of standard monetary and fiscal policies. [5 marks]
answer: Demand expansion raises output on the horizontal AS segment, but raises only prices on either vertical segment until a regime boundary is reached.
solution: Expansionary monetary or fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand to the right. If equilibrium lies on the horizontal AS segment at $P_0=\bar W/A$ with spare labour, this raises employment and output without changing the price level, until full employment is reached. If equilibrium is already on the full-employment vertical segment, further expansion raises only the price level. If it lies on the lower-output vertical segment at $Y=\bar K$ with $P<P_0$, a small expansion initially raises only $P$; output begins to increase only when demand is strong enough to bring the price to $P_0$. Contraction has the reverse regime-dependent effects. Thus it is not correct to state that demand policy always changes output in this model.
hint: Consider where the downward-sloping AD curve intersects each of the three AS segments.

stem: In a discrete-time Solow model $Y_t=K_t^\alpha L_t^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$. Competitive factors receive marginal products. Households save a fraction $0<s<1$ of disposable income, and all private savings are invested. There is no depreciation. Labour grows at rate $n>0$. Let $k_t=K_t/L_t$. The government taxes interest earnings at rate $0<\tau<1$, does not tax wages, and spends all tax revenue on consumption. (i) Derive aggregate wage earnings, interest earnings and savings in terms of $Y_t$. (ii) Derive the law of motion for $k_t$. (iii) Find its steady state and its response to $\tau$. [14 marks]
answer: Wages $(1-\alpha)Y_t$, gross interest $\alpha Y_t$, savings $s(1-\tau\alpha)Y_t$; $k_{t+1}=[k_t+s(1-\tau\alpha)k_t^\alpha]/(1+n)$; positive $k^*=[s(1-\tau\alpha)/n]^{1/(1-\alpha)}$, decreasing in $\tau$.
solution: The marginal products are $w_t=(1-\alpha)(K_t/L_t)^\alpha$ and $r_t=\alpha(K_t/L_t)^{\alpha-1}$. Thus total wage earnings are $(1-\alpha)Y_t$ and total gross interest earnings are $\alpha Y_t$. Disposable household income is $(1-\alpha)Y_t+(1-\tau)\alpha Y_t=(1-\tau\alpha)Y_t$, so $S_t=s(1-\tau\alpha)Y_t$. Since tax revenue is consumed rather than invested, $K_{t+1}=K_t+S_t$. Dividing by $L_{t+1}=(1+n)L_t$ gives $k_{t+1}=[k_t+s(1-\tau\alpha)k_t^\alpha]/(1+n)$. At a positive steady state, $nk^*=s(1-\tau\alpha)(k^*)^\alpha$, yielding the expression above. Its logarithmic derivative is $\partial\log k^*/\partial\tau=-\alpha/[(1-\alpha)(1-\tau\alpha)]<0$. A higher tax reduces private saving and hence positive steady-state capital. Zero capital is also an absorbing steady state if admitted; the displayed solution is the economically relevant positive one.
hint: Use Cobb-Douglas factor shares, then divide capital accumulation by next period's labour force.

stem: In a discrete-time Solow model $Y_t=K_t^\alpha L_t^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$. Competitive factors receive marginal products. Households save a fraction $0<s<1$ of disposable income, and all private savings are invested. There is no depreciation. Labour grows at rate $n>0$. Let $k_t=K_t/L_t$. Interest is still taxed at rate $\tau$ and wages are untaxed, but all tax revenue is now invested by the government. (i) Find total investment. (ii) Derive the new law of motion. (iii) Find the new positive steady state $k^{**}$ and compare it with $k^*$. (iv) Determine how $k^{**}$ changes with $\tau$, and explain the difference from part(a). [16 marks]
answer: $I_t=[s+(1-s)\tau\alpha]Y_t$ and $k^{**}=\{[s+(1-s)\tau\alpha]/n\}^{1/(1-\alpha)}>k^*$; $k^{**}$ increases with $\tau$.
solution: Private saving remains $s(1-\tau\alpha)Y_t$, but government investment adds $\tau\alpha Y_t$. Therefore aggregate investment is $I_t=[s+(1-s)\tau\alpha]Y_t$. The new accumulation equation is $k_{t+1}=\{k_t+[s+(1-s)\tau\alpha]k_t^\alpha\}/(1+n)$. The positive steady state is $k^{**}=\{[s+(1-s)\tau\alpha]/n\}^{1/(1-\alpha)}$. It exceeds $k^*$ because their effective investment coefficients differ by $\tau\alpha>0$: revenue that was previously consumed is now invested. Moreover $\partial\log k^{**}/\partial\tau=(1-s)\alpha/\{(1-\alpha)[s+(1-s)\tau\alpha]\}>0$. Although taxation reduces private saving by $s\alpha$ per unit increase in the tax rate, government investment rises by $\alpha$, leaving a positive net effect $(1-s)\alpha$. This reverses the response in part(a).
hint: Add government investment to private saving; do not count the tax revenue as both household disposable income and public investment.
notes: Question5(b) starts on PDF page13 and continues on page14.

stem: An individual lives for two periods. First-period wage income is $W$, personal savings are $s$, and the gross interest factor is $R>1$. The government takes a first-period lump-sum tax $T$ and returns exactly $T$ in period2. Lifetime utility is $u(c_1)+\beta u(c_2)$, with $0<\beta<1$ and $u$ strictly increasing and strictly concave. Specify the utility maximization problem and budget constraint. Derive the first-order condition and interpret it economically. [9 marks]
answer: Maximize $u(W-T-s)+\beta u(Rs+T)$ over feasible saving; an interior optimum satisfies $u'(c_1)=\beta R u'(c_2)$.
solution: The two period budgets are $c_1=W-T-s$ and $c_2=Rs+T$. Equivalently $c_1+c_2/R=W-T+T/R$. Choose $s$ to maximize $u(W-T-s)+\beta u(Rs+T)$ subject to nonnegative consumption (and $s\geq0$ if borrowing is disallowed). Differentiating at an interior optimum gives $-u'(W-T-s)+\beta R u'(Rs+T)=0$. Strict concavity makes an interior solution unique. The condition equates the marginal utility lost by saving one additional first-period rupee to the discounted utility gained from its $R$ rupees of second-period consumption. At a binding constraint a one-sided/KKT inequality replaces the equality.
hint: Write both consumption levels as functions of personal saving before differentiating.
notes: The derivative conclusions use a differentiable interior optimum with positive consumption. The source does not impose Inada conditions or explicitly rule out binding saving/consumption constraints.

stem: An individual lives for two periods. First-period wage income is $W$, personal savings are $s$, and the gross interest factor is $R>1$. The government takes a first-period lump-sum tax $T$ and returns exactly $T$ in period2. Lifetime utility is $u(c_1)+\beta u(c_2)$, with $0<\beta<1$ and $u$ strictly increasing and strictly concave. Would a more myopic individual save more or less? Verify by determining the sign of $ds/d\beta$. [5 marks]
answer: At an interior optimum $ds/d\beta>0$; a more myopic (smaller $\beta$) individual saves less.
solution: Set $F(s,T,\beta)=u'(W-T-s)-\beta R u'(Rs+T)=0$. Write $A=-u''(c_1)>0$ and $B=-u''(c_2)>0$. Then $F_s=A+\beta R^2B>0$ and $F_\beta=-Ru'(c_2)<0$. Hence $ds/d\beta=Ru'(c_2)/(A+\beta R^2B)>0$. A larger discount factor increases the value attached to future consumption, inducing higher personal saving; a more myopic individual has a smaller discount factor and saves less.
hint: Differentiate the Euler equation implicitly, keeping $W,T,R$ fixed.
notes: The derivative conclusions use a differentiable interior optimum with positive consumption. The source does not impose Inada conditions or explicitly rule out binding saving/consumption constraints.

stem: An individual lives for two periods. First-period wage income is $W$, personal savings are $s$, and the gross interest factor is $R>1$. The government takes a first-period lump-sum tax $T$ and returns exactly $T$ in period2. Lifetime utility is $u(c_1)+\beta u(c_2)$, with $0<\beta<1$ and $u$ strictly increasing and strictly concave. Does government-mandated saving $T$ increase or decrease personal saving? Verify by finding the sign of $ds/dT$. [6 marks]
solution: Using the Euler-equation function from part(a), its partial derivative in $T$ is $F_T=-u''(c_1)-\beta Ru''(c_2)=A+\beta RB>0$. Since $F_s=A+\beta R^2B>0$, implicit differentiation gives $ds/dT=-F_T/F_s=-(A+\beta RB)/(A+\beta R^2B)<0$. The compulsory transfer toward period2 crowds out personal saving. It also reduces lifetime wealth because the government returns no interest, so the crowding-out is not a simple one-for-one adjustment.
hint: The tax lowers first-period resources and raises second-period resources. Include both effects in $F_T$.
notes: The derivative conclusions use a differentiable interior optimum with positive consumption. The source does not impose Inada conditions or explicitly rule out binding saving/consumption constraints.

stem: An individual lives for two periods. First-period wage income is $W$, personal savings are $s$, and the gross interest factor is $R>1$. The government takes a first-period lump-sum tax $T$ and returns exactly $T$ in period2. Lifetime utility is $u(c_1)+\beta u(c_2)$, with $0<\beta<1$ and $u$ strictly increasing and strictly concave. One rupee of period2 benefit could be financed privately by saving $1/R$ in period1. Does mandated saving cause personal saving to fall at a rate greater or smaller than $1/R$? Verify. [4 marks]
answer: The magnitude exceeds $1/R$ but is below1: $1/R<-ds/dT<1$.
solution: The crowding-out magnitude from part(c) is $(A+\beta RB)/(A+\beta R^2B)$. It is smaller than1 because the denominator exceeds the numerator by $\beta R(R-1)B>0$. It is greater than $1/R$ because $R(A+\beta RB)-(A+\beta R^2B)=(R-1)A>0$. Therefore $-1<ds/dT<-1/R$. A transfer of one rupee in period2 by itself would replace $1/R$ rupees of private saving, but the associated first-period tax is larger than that present value and reduces lifetime wealth. The combined response cuts saving by more than $1/R$ but by less than one rupee.
hint: Compare the ratio from part(c) with both $1/R$ and1 by multiplying by its positive denominator.
notes: The derivative conclusions use a differentiable interior optimum with positive consumption. The source does not impose Inada conditions or explicitly rule out binding saving/consumption constraints.

stem: An individual lives for two periods. First-period wage income is $W$, personal savings are $s$, and the gross interest factor is $R>1$. The government takes a first-period lump-sum tax $T$ and returns exactly $T$ in period2. Lifetime utility is $u(c_1)+\beta u(c_2)$, with $0<\beta<1$ and $u$ strictly increasing and strictly concave. Prove that more myopic individuals reduce their personal savings at a higher rate in response to a rise in $T$. [6 marks]
answer: The claim does not follow from the stated assumptions and is false in general. Log utility gives the opposite ranking.
solution: Take the permitted utility $u(c)=\log c$ and an interior solution. The Euler equation gives $s=\beta W/(1+\beta)-(\beta R+1)T/[R(1+\beta)]$. Therefore $ds/dT=-(\beta R+1)/[R(1+\beta)]$. The derivative of its absolute magnitude with respect to $\beta$ is $(R-1)/[R(1+\beta)^2]>0$. Thus a larger discount factor (less myopia), not a smaller one, produces the larger absolute cut in saving in this example. For example $R=2,W=10,T=1$ yields interior savings at both $\beta=1/4$ and $\beta=1/2$; the crowding-out magnitudes are $3/5$ and $2/3$, respectively. More myopia therefore yields a smaller cut. In general, the curvatures $u''(c_1)$ and $u''(c_2)$ in part(c) are evaluated at consumption levels that also change with $\beta$, so one cannot hold them fixed to infer the comparative static requested here. Additional restrictions, or a corrected claim, are necessary.
hint: Test the proposed universal claim using $u(c)=\log c$ before trying to prove it.
notes: The printed claim is mathematically false for the stated general class of utility functions. It must not be presented as proved. A log-utility counterexample is given, with strictly positive interior saving and consumption.

stem: Let $C=\{(x,y):0\leq x\leq1,\ 0\leq y\leq1,\ y\leq x\}$ and maximize $ax+by$ over $C$. For $a\neq0$ and $b\neq0$, show that an optimal solution can be chosen from $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1)$. Describe all coefficient values for which each vertex is optimal. [20 marks]
answer: $(0,0)$ is optimal iff $a\leq0$ and $a+b\leq0$; $(1,0)$ iff $a\geq0$ and $b\leq0$; $(1,1)$ iff $b\geq0$ and $a+b\geq0$, subject to the stated nonzero coefficients.
solution: The feasible set is the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1)$. Every feasible point can be expressed as $(x,y)=(1-x)(0,0)+(x-y)(1,0)+y(1,1)$, with nonnegative coefficients summing to1. Its objective is therefore a convex combination of the vertex values $0,a,a+b$, so at least one vertex maximizes the objective. Comparing these values gives the stated conditions. Because $a,b\neq0$, the middle vertex is uniquely optimal exactly when $a>0,b<0$. For the origin, strict uniqueness requires $a<0,a+b<0$; for $(1,1)$ it requires $b>0,a+b>0$. At $a+b=0$ with $a<0<b$, every point on the diagonal edge from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$ is optimal as well. Thus existence of a vertex optimum does not imply that every optimum is a vertex.
hint: Write any feasible point as a convex combination of the three vertices and compare the values $0,a,a+b$.
notes: The feasible-set definition starts on PDF page14. The statement is interpreted as existence of a vertex optimum; nonvertex optima occur on a tie edge.

stem: Let $C=\{(x,y):0\leq x\leq1,\ 0\leq y\leq1,\ y\leq x\}$ and maximize $ax+by$ over $C$. Suppose $a$ and $b$ are independently drawn from $[-1,1]$ with common cumulative distribution function $F$. What is the probability that the unique optimum is $(1,0)$? [10 marks]
answer: $P=(1-F(0))F(0^-)$; for a continuous cdf this is $F(0)[1-F(0)]$.
solution: The vertex $(1,0)$ is uniquely optimal iff $a>0$ and $b<0$. By independence the probability is $P(a>0)P(b<0)=[1-F(0)]F(0^-)$, where $F(0^-)=\lim_{t\uparrow0}F(t)$. If $F$ is continuous at zero, this reduces to $F(0)[1-F(0)]$. For a uniform distribution on $[-1,1]$ it is $1/4$, but uniformity is not assumed in the question. An atom at zero must be excluded from the strict negative event.
hint: Use strict inequalities for uniqueness, and distinguish $P(b<0)$ from $P(b\leq0)$ when the distribution may have atoms.

stem: Real coefficients satisfy $A\neq0$, $a\neq0$ and $|ax^2+bx+c|\leq|Ax^2+Bx+C|$ for every real $x$. Also $B^2-4AC>0$. Argue that $|A|\geq|a|$. [5 marks]
solution: For $x\neq0$, divide the inequality by $x^2>0$. This gives $|a+b/x+c/x^2|\leq|A+B/x+C/x^2|$. Taking $x\to\infty$ and using continuity of absolute value yields $|a|\leq|A|$.
hint: Compare leading coefficients by letting $|x|$ become large.

stem: Real coefficients satisfy $A\neq0$, $a\neq0$ and $|ax^2+bx+c|\leq|Ax^2+Bx+C|$ for every real $x$. Also $B^2-4AC>0$. Show that $b^2-4ac>0$. [10 marks]
answer: The smaller quadratic has the same two distinct real roots as the larger one, hence positive discriminant.
solution: Since $B^2-4AC>0$, $G(x)=Ax^2+Bx+C$ has two distinct real roots $r_1,r_2$. At either root the assumed inequality forces $|ar_i^2+br_i+c|\leq0$, so the quadratic $g(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ also vanishes at both. Because $a\neq0$, it is a genuine quadratic with two distinct real roots. Therefore its discriminant $b^2-4ac$ is strictly positive.
hint: Evaluate the absolute-value inequality at each root of $Ax^2+Bx+C$.

stem: Real coefficients satisfy $A\neq0$, $a\neq0$ and $|ax^2+bx+c|\leq|Ax^2+Bx+C|$ for every real $x$. Also $B^2-4AC>0$. Show that $B^2-4AC\geq b^2-4ac$. [15 marks]
solution: By part(b), both quadratics have the same two distinct roots. Hence $ax^2+bx+c=\lambda(Ax^2+Bx+C)$, where $\lambda=a/A\neq0$. Thus $b=\lambda B$ and $c=\lambda C$. Part(a) implies $|\lambda|\leq1$. Consequently $b^2-4ac=\lambda^2(B^2-4AC)\leq B^2-4AC$, since the latter discriminant is positive.
hint: Two genuine quadratics with the same two distinct roots are proportional.

stem: Let $\mathcal F$ be a class of functions from $[0,\infty)$ to $[0,\infty)$. It contains $f_1(x)=e^x-1$ and $f_2(x)=\ln(x+1)$. It is closed under addition and composition. It is also closed under $f-g$ whenever $f,g\in\mathcal F$ and $f(x)\geq g(x)$ for every $x\geq0$. For every positive integer $n$, show that $h(x)=nx$ belongs to $\mathcal F$. [5 marks]
answer: Compose $f_1$ with $f_2$ to obtain $x$, then add $n$ copies.
solution: Closure under composition implies $f_1(f_2(x))=\exp(\ln(1+x))-1=x$ is in $\mathcal F$. Repeated closure under addition then shows that the sum of $n$ copies of this identity function, namely $nx$, is in $\mathcal F$ for every positive integer $n$.
hint: First construct the identity function using the two given functions.

stem: Let $\mathcal F$ be a class of functions from $[0,\infty)$ to $[0,\infty)$. It contains $f_1(x)=e^x-1$ and $f_2(x)=\ln(x+1)$. It is closed under addition and composition. It is also closed under $f-g$ whenever $f,g\in\mathcal F$ and $f(x)\geq g(x)$ for every $x\geq0$. If $f,g\in\mathcal F$, prove that $\ln(f(x)+1)$ and $\ln(g(x)+1)$ belong to $\mathcal F$. [5 marks]
answer: These are the compositions $f_2\circ f$ and $f_2\circ g$.
solution: Because $f$ and $g$ are nonnegative, both compositions with $f_2(t)=\ln(1+t)$ are defined on the required domain and remain nonnegative. Closure under composition gives $f_2(f(x))=\ln(1+f(x))$ and $f_2(g(x))=\ln(1+g(x))$ in $\mathcal F$.
hint: Apply the given logarithm function by composition.

stem: Let $\mathcal F$ be a class of functions from $[0,\infty)$ to $[0,\infty)$. It contains $f_1(x)=e^x-1$ and $f_2(x)=\ln(x+1)$. It is closed under addition and composition. It is also closed under $f-g$ whenever $f,g\in\mathcal F$ and $f(x)\geq g(x)$ for every $x\geq0$. If $f,g\in\mathcal F$, prove that $f(x)g(x)+f(x)+g(x)$ belongs to $\mathcal F$. [15 marks]
answer: Compose $f_1$ with $\ln(1+f)+\ln(1+g)$.
solution: Part(b) and addition show $H(x)=\ln(1+f(x))+\ln(1+g(x))$ is in $\mathcal F$. Closure under composition with $f_1$ then gives $e^{H(x)}-1\in\mathcal F$. Algebraically, $e^{H(x)}-1=(1+f(x))(1+g(x))-1=f(x)g(x)+f(x)+g(x)$.
hint: A sum of logarithms becomes a product after applying $e^t-1$.

stem: Let $\mathcal F$ be a class of functions from $[0,\infty)$ to $[0,\infty)$. It contains $f_1(x)=e^x-1$ and $f_2(x)=\ln(x+1)$. It is closed under addition and composition. It is also closed under $f-g$ whenever $f,g\in\mathcal F$ and $f(x)\geq g(x)$ for every $x\geq0$. If $f,g\in\mathcal F$, prove that $f(x)g(x)$ belongs to $\mathcal F$. [5 marks]
answer: Subtract $f+g$ from the nonnegative dominating function $fg+f+g$.
solution: By part(c), $fg+f+g$ is in $\mathcal F$, and by addition $f+g$ is in $\mathcal F$. Since $f,g\geq0$, their product is nonnegative and therefore $fg+f+g\geq f+g$ pointwise. The permitted subtraction rule applies, yielding $(fg+f+g)-(f+g)=fg\in\mathcal F$.
hint: Check the pointwise dominance condition before using subtraction.
